name: Yara Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Yara, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my brother-in-law Raúl's firm, Reyes and Sons, though now it's Reyes and Sons and me. We do repairs on old buildings, chapels, farmhouses, the old school house, so this month it's new sash windows and a rotten oak lintel at St Anne's chapel out on the valley road. I carry, I sand, I cut what Raúl marks, and I'm learning to make a sash box, slowly. I'm fifty-eight and I only started four years ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to it so late?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Ernesto was a bricklayer, and five years ago he fell from a scaffold and hurt his back badly. He can't work now. I'd raised our four children at home, I'd never had a wage, and Raúl said, come on, family looks after family. So I'm the one earning, we rent, and we've got less than a month's money saved. I have the old kind of phone, calls and texts. My granddaughter laughs at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it. I'd say it after Mass to the other women, because a lot of them were worried about their grandchildren's jobs. I don't go on the internet, so that's as far as it would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it changes nothing for me, and that's a mercy. The work on old chapels won't be done by a computer anyway. I've got enough trouble with my wrists and the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going to work every day, keep learning from Raúl, and keep putting a bit in the tin for Christmas. I wouldn't change anything. I'd thank God, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weight that was never really on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why are you sure old chapels are safe from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every one is different. The lintel at St Anne's, the oak's been there three hundred years and it's moved, so nothing's square, and Raúl reads it like a book. A machine wants everything the same, and nothing in an old building is the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a lot of the women were worried about their grandchildren. Are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. My grandson Mateo wants to work in offices, with computers, and that's where they say it'll hit. I tell him learn a trade, like his grandfather, but he says nobody wants to carry bricks anymore.

S0.say: I'd say good, I never trusted it, mostly to the other women after Mass. I don't go on the internet, so it wouldn't go further than that.
S0.think: It changes nothing for me, and that's a mercy, because computers won't be repairing old chapels. My real troubles are my wrists and the bills.
S0.do: Keeps going to work at her brother-in-law's heritage repair firm and keeps learning from him. Puts a little in the tin for Christmas and changes nothing else.
S0.feel: Calm, as if a weight that was never really on her has gone.
S0.quote: A machine wants everything the same, and nothing in an old building is the same.
S0.fieldNote: Yara's world is family, church and the old buildings Raúl's firm repairs, and she sees AI as far from all three. She's the household's only earner, so bills and her wrists matter more than technology. Her faith in the uniqueness of old buildings is strong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have always had to adapt, and families should help each other through it, not wait for the government. I'd say it at church and to my children. My son-in-law would probably argue, he likes the government to do everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Raúl's firm would be all right for a while, because people who own old chapels want craftsmen, not gadgets. But if Raúl's sons start using tablets and machines to speed things up, there's less need for a slow helper like me. That's what would keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder and make sure I'm useful, maybe do the cleaning up and the sanding nobody likes. I wouldn't do courses on computers, I wouldn't know where to start. I'd wait and see what Raúl decides, he's the head of the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I trust Raúl, but trust doesn't pay the rent if the work isn't there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Raúl had to let you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd understand, it's his business. I'd ask at the church whether anyone needed a cleaner or someone to sit with old people. And Ernesto and I would go to our daughter Lucía, she's always said we can come to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the tablets yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My granddaughter tried to show me on hers once and I pressed the wrong thing and called someone in another country. I'd leave the tablets to Raúl's boys and keep my hands on the wood.

S1.say: I'd say people have always had to adapt and families should help each other, not wait for the government. I'd say it at church and to my children.
S1.think: Raúl's firm would be fine for a while, because people with old chapels want craftsmen, not gadgets. But if his sons speed things up with tablets, there's less need for a slow helper like me.
S1.do: Works harder and takes on the cleaning and sanding nobody likes to stay useful. Avoids computer courses and waits to see what her brother-in-law decides for the business.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, because trust doesn't pay the rent if the work isn't there.
S1.quote: I trust Raúl, but trust doesn't pay the rent if the work isn't there.
S1.fieldNote: Yara puts family before state, and her backup plans are church work and her daughter. She won't touch tablets. Her loyalty to Raúl is deep but she's clear-eyed about its limits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the big companies playing God, and it's wrong. I'd say families and churches will have to hold people together, because the government can't do it all. And I'd vote for whoever promised to keep people in real work, not just send cheques.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be terrified. I'm the only one earning, Ernesto can't work, and in 2028 I'd be sixty with less than a month saved. If even old chapels can be fixed by a robot, there's nothing for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Lucía and her husband first and say we may have to come to you. I'd stop everything we don't need, the TV package, Ernesto's cigarettes, which he'd hate, the bus pass if I can walk. And I'd ask the priest about any work the parish has, cleaning, cooking, anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but I'd pray. Prayer doesn't fix it, but it stops me shaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ernesto that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we've had worse, we had the fall. He'd be quiet, he's been quiet since the accident, he hates that I'm the one working. I'd make his tea and we'd sit, and I'd not tell him how scared I was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. Would you try anything new before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not new, no. I'd work every extra hour Raúl could give me and put it all by. And I'd ask the women at church to keep their ears open for any job a person still has to do, because that's how things get done where I live.

S2.say: I'd say it's the big companies playing God and it's wrong; families and churches will have to hold people together. I'd vote for whoever promised to keep people in real work, not just send cheques.
S2.think: I'd be terrified, as the only earner with Ernesto unable to work, sixty and less than a month saved. If robots can fix old chapels, there's nothing left for me.
S2.do: Asks her daughter and son-in-law if they could take her and her husband in. Cuts the TV package, his cigarettes and possibly the bus pass, and asks the priest about parish work.
S2.feel: Frightened, steadied a little by prayer.
S2.quote: Prayer doesn't fix it, but it stops me shaking.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI threatens Yara's role as sole earner, and she turns to daughter, priest and parish rather than the state. She'd hide her fear from her husband, who already feels shame about not working. She blames big tech companies in moral terms: 'playing God'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for the young ones to learn a trade the machines can't do, and families should push them. For people my age, the churches and families will have to look after us. I'd say it to my grandchildren especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gets me to sixty-three. Ernesto gets a small payment for his back, but we couldn't live on it. I'd still be frightened, more than I'd let on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Raúl as long as he'd have me, and I'd ask him honestly what he thinks will happen. I'd try to put twenty a week by, which means no more coffee at the market on Saturday. And I'd ask Lucía now whether moving in with her would be possible, so it's settled, not a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but at least I can see it coming. I don't like surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn anything new in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. Raúl says the computer people will have it all on screens, and I can't even send a picture on my phone. I'd rather spend those years doing what I can do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about moving in with Lucía?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be hard, it's her home and her husband's. But that's what families are for, we took in my mother for six years. I'd cook and help with the little ones, so we'd be paying our way.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time for the young ones to learn a trade machines can't do, and families should push them. People my age will need churches and families to look after us.
S3.think: Five years gets me to sixty-three, and Ernesto's small payment for his back isn't enough to live on. I'd still be frightened, more than I'd let on.
S3.do: Keeps working for Raúl as long as she can and asks him honestly what he expects. Saves twenty a week by giving up Saturday coffee at the market and settles a possible move to her daughter's early.
S3.feel: Scared, but glad to see it coming because she dislikes surprises.
S3.quote: Raúl says the computer people will have it all on screens, and I can't even send a picture on my phone.
S3.fieldNote: Five years helps Yara plan, but not change: she won't learn new tools and would rather spend the time on what she does well. Her husband's small payment doesn't cover them, so she stays alarmed. Her advice to grandchildren shows her belief in learning a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and families can plan. The young ones should get apprenticeships in things a person must do. I'd say to Raúl's sons, train up now while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years and I'm sixty-eight, on my pension, so maybe I'd get through. But the pension won't be much, because I didn't have a wage for most of my life. So I'd still worry about the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep putting a bit by each week, and stay close to my family and church. I'd wait to see what the big firms do. If old chapels are still standing without robots in five years, I'd stop worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but quieter. It feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would your pension be small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I raised four children at home and nobody paid me for that. Ernesto's work was going to be our pension, and then he fell. So it's my few years with Raúl and what the state gives, and that's not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family would you worry about most in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandchildren, the ones still in school. I'll have had my life, but they'll be starting theirs in a world I don't understand. I'd want them near family, near the church, with something solid in their hands.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and families can plan. Young people should get apprenticeships in work a person must do, and Raúl's sons should train up now.
S4.think: At sixty-eight I'd be on my pension and might get through. But it won't be much, since I didn't have a wage for most of my life, so I'd still worry about the end.
S4.do: Keeps working, saves a little each week and stays close to family and church. Waits to see what big firms do and would stop worrying if old chapels still needed people in five years.
S4.feel: Worried, but more quietly, because it feels far away.
S4.quote: Because I raised four children at home and nobody paid me for that.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Yara reaches pension age, but her years of unpaid work at home mean a small pension. Her husband's accident wiped out their retirement plan. She stays anxious and leans on family, faith and waiting to see.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. I'm the only one earning and I'd have nothing to fall back on. What would help is real work for people like me, even part-time, and support for families who take in their parents, not handouts but help for families doing their duty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who never had a wage. Women like me who raised children and then had to start at the bottom at fifty-four. We're not in anyone's numbers.

portrait: Yara Reyes is a 58-year-old trainee on her brother-in-law's heritage repair crew, working on old chapels and farmhouses. She started at fifty-four after her bricklayer husband was injured, and she's now the family's only earner, with a basic phone and no interest in AI. She's calm if AI stalls, uneasy under steady change, and alarmed by both fast AGI pictures, turning first to her daughter, her priest and prayer. With ten years she reaches her pension but still worries, because years of unpaid work at home leave her with little.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because she's the only one earning and has nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Real work, even part-time, for people like her, and support for families who take in their parents, framed as help for families, not handouts.
